message.content:
Below is a concise summary of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you need help with a specific situation, consider consulting an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit. | Keep a written receipt when you pay the deposit. Ask for a written itemized list of any deductions before you move out. | | **Notice Requirements** | • 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month leases.
• 60‑day notice if the lease term is longer than 30 days. | Get the notice in writing and keep a copy. If you receive a notice that is too short, you may be able to challenge it. | | **Habitability** | Landlords must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition and comply with building codes. | Document any repairs needed (photos, written requests). If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct, but do so only after following proper procedures. | | **Rent Payment** | Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed but cannot exceed 5% of the monthly rent. | Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Eviction Process** | Evictions require a court order. The landlord must file a complaint, serve you, and obtain a judgment. You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | Respond promptly to any notices. Attend all court hearings and bring evidence (e.g., receipts, correspondence). | | **Privacy / Entry** | Landlords must give at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of any entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you may be able to claim a violation. | | **Discrimination** | Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | Either party can terminate a lease by giving proper notice (as above). Some leases include “no‑cause” termination clauses that allow the landlord to end the tenancy early. | Review your lease for any “no‑cause” clauses. If you believe a clause is unfair, consult a lawyer. | | **Repair & Deduct** | If the landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair them yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the correct procedure (written notice, reasonable timeframe, etc.). | Keep receipts and document the problem. Notify the landlord in writing before making any repairs. | | **Rent Control / Rent Increase** | Texas has no statewide rent‑control law. Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term, but they must give proper notice (usually 30 days). | Verify the notice period in your lease. If the increase is unreasonable, you can negotiate or seek legal counsel. | ### Where to Get Help | Resource | What it offers | How to access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant disputes, consumer complaints. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Handles discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal clinics, mediation services. | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” + your city. | | **Legal Aid Services** | Free legal representation for qualifying tenants. | https://www.lawhelptexas.org/ | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | National fair housing hotline. | https://www.hud.gov/ | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the lease carefully** – note the rent amount, due date, security deposit, notice periods, and any special clauses. 2. **Get a written receipt** for the security deposit and any initial payments. 3. **Document the property’s condition** – take photos or videos of existing damage and keep a written inventory. 4. **Ask for a copy of the lease** – keep a signed copy for your records. If you have a specific question—like how to handle a late notice, what to do if your landlord refuses to make repairs, or whether a particular clause is enforceable—feel free to ask!
